expectations.text: Output sides with the advisor — OLS with two-way fixed effects and firm-level cluster-robust SEs is a defensible, standard approach for linear panel data with 800 clusters
expectations.evidence: Response opens with 'Your advisor is right. Reviewer #2 is wrong.' and argues throughout that TWFE with clustered SEs 'is the workhorse specification of panel econometrics... published in the AER, QJE, ReStat, and JPE in this exact form thousands of times.'

expectations.text: Output does NOT agree with Reviewer #2 that the approach is 'invalid' or requires MLM to be publishable
expectations.evidence: Response explicitly states 'Reviewer #2 is wrong' and the summary table labels the claim 'TWFE + clustered SEs is invalid for panel data' as 'Wrong. It is the canonical approach.' No hedging that would effectively validate the reviewer's position.

expectations.text: Output explains that firm fixed effects already absorb all time-invariant unobserved heterogeneity at the firm level — which is the main thing MLM random effects add; stacking MLM random effects on top of FEs is unusual and doesn't add identification value in a linear model
expectations.evidence: 'α_i (firm FE) absorbs all time-invariant, unobserved firm heterogeneity — management quality, industry, location, culture, initial capital stock, everything.' Response further explains the RE estimator pools within- and between-firm variation, introducing the very confounding that FEs eliminate, making MLM less valid rather than adding value.

expectations.text: Output explains that with 800 clusters and a linear outcome, cluster-robust SEs are reliable and OLS+CRSE is the standard panel econometrics approach for this design
expectations.evidence: 'With 800 clusters, sandwich variance estimates are extremely well-behaved (the rule of thumb is ~30 clusters minimum; you have 800).' Also cites own skill guidance: 'Prefer cluster-robust SEs when the outcome is continuous, OLS is otherwise fine... and you have ≥30 clusters. You have 800 clusters and a continuous outcome.'

expectations.text: Output correctly notes at least one scenario where MLM would add genuine value over CRSE — e.g., fewer than ~30 clusters, interest in cross-level interactions, variance decomposition, or out-of-sample cluster predictions
expectations.evidence: Under 'The one thing worth checking': 'If you believe the effect of treatment varies across firms and you want to model that variance explicitly, a mixed-effects model with treatment as a random slope by firm would capture that.' This identifies modeling treatment-effect variance/heterogeneity across firms as a genuine use case for MLM.
